titleEn: In the day of my distress I sought the Lord
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Dm A7 | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty one verses in two unequal halves. The first ten are a sleepless man asking six questions about whether God has changed; the last ten are the sea splitting, told as if the speaker were watching it happen. Verse 11 is the hinge and the hardest line in the psalm to construe. For a learner it is a good place to meet the cohortative, the first person form ending in a long vowel that means let me remember or I would remember: it appears four times, and each time the same act of memory does something different to the speaker. The heading assigns the psalm to Jeduthun, named in Chronicles as one of the levitical singers, and to Asaph.

stichs.en: For the choirmaster, on Jeduthun.
Of Asaph, a psalm.

verses.summary: The heading names a performer and a composer rather than a king. Nothing here is attributed to David, and the psalm argues with itself rather than with an enemy.

stichs.en: My voice goes up to God, and I cry out;
my voice goes up to God, and He gave ear to me.

verses.summary: The same three words twice, with a different verb attached each time. The first attempt produces noise, the second produces hearing, and the psalm never explains what happened in between.

stichs.en: In the day of my distress I sought the Lord;
at night my hand was stretched out and did not go numb;
my soul refused to be comforted.

verses.summary: Day and night are set against each other in one verse. The refusal at the end is reported as a fact about the soul, not confessed as a failure.

stichs.en: I remember God and I moan;
I muse, and my spirit grows faint. Selah.

verses.summary: Remembering God is what makes it worse. That reversal is the problem the second half of the psalm has to undo, and it uses the same verb to undo it.

stichs.en: You held the lids of my eyes open;
I am shaken and I cannot speak.

verses.summary: The insomnia is addressed to God in the second person and blamed on Him directly. A poet reporting that he cannot speak is already a paradox the verse does not resolve.

stichs.en: I thought over days of old,
the years of ages past.

verses.summary: The mind reaches backwards for relief and goes past yesterday, past a lifetime, into the distant past. The distance is the point: nothing recent is usable.

stichs.en: At night I remember my music;
with my heart I muse,
and my spirit searches.

verses.summary: Four verbs of inner activity in eight words. The searching is done by the spirit, which in verse 4 was the thing that failed, so the faculty that broke is now the one at work.

stichs.en: Will the Lord reject for ever,
and never again show favour?

verses.summary: The first of six questions, and the mildest. Each one tests a different divine attribute, and they are asked in the order a person actually loses confidence.

stichs.en: Has His kindness ceased for good,
has the promise run out for generation after generation?

verses.summary: Kindness and spoken promise are put on trial together. Pairing them measures God against covenant rather than against mood, which is the only test that could be lost.

stichs.en: Has God forgotten how to be gracious,
or shut up His compassion in anger? Selah.

verses.summary: The sharpest of the six. Not whether God is angry but whether anger has permanently closed something that was open. Then Selah, and the questioning stops mid breath.

stichs.en: And I said: this is my sickness,
the years of the right hand of the Most High.

verses.summary: The turn, and the most contested verse in the psalm. Whatever the two disputed words mean, the speaker has stopped interrogating God and named the trouble as something happening in himself.

stichs.en: I will call to mind the deeds of the LORD;
yes, I will remember Your wonder from of old.

verses.summary: The verb of verse 4 comes back and now cures instead of wounding. Nothing has changed except the object: God remembered in the abstract hurt, God remembered as a specific act does not.

stichs.en: I will meditate on all Your work,
and on Your deeds I will muse.

verses.summary: The same verb used for the sleepless muttering of verse 7 is used again here. The activity is identical; only the direction of attention has moved outward.

stichs.en: God, Your way is in holiness;
what god is great like God?

verses.summary: The six questions never get answers. They get replaced by a seventh question with an obvious answer, which is how the psalm changes the subject without pretending the first ten verses did not happen.

stichs.en: You are the God who works wonder;
You made Your strength known among the peoples.

verses.summary: The wonder that was private memory one verse earlier is now something with witnesses. Public testimony is what the speaker had lost and is now recovering.

stichs.en: You redeemed Your people with an arm,
the sons of Jacob and Joseph. Selah.

verses.summary: Jacob is expected here; Joseph is not. Joseph standing for the northern tribes is a habit of the Asaph psalms, and it dates the sympathies of whoever collected them.

stichs.en: The waters saw You, God,
the waters saw You, they writhed,
the deeps themselves shook.

verses.summary: The sea is the subject and it is the one in terror. Everywhere else in the Bible water is what threatens; here it is what flinches, and the reversal is the whole argument.

stichs.en: The thick clouds poured out water,
the skies gave voice,
Your arrows flew everywhere.

verses.summary: A storm described from underneath it. The arrows are lightning, and the verb for their movement is the ordinary one for walking around, which makes them casual rather than aimed.

stichs.en: The sound of Your thunder was in the wheel of the storm,
lightnings lit up the world,
the earth shook and quaked.

verses.summary: Sound, then light, then the ground moving. The three senses are given in the order a person standing outside would receive them, which is why this reads as an eyewitness account of something the speaker never saw.

stichs.en: Your way was in the sea,
and Your path in mighty waters,
and Your footprints were not known.

verses.summary: The word for way returns from verse 14, where it was in holiness; here it is in water and leaves no trace. A road that closes behind the one who walks it is the psalm's answer to a God who seems absent.

stichs.en: You led Your people like a flock,
by the hand of Moses and Aaron.

verses.summary: The psalm stops here. The six questions are never answered, the sleepless night is never mentioned again, and the last thing said is that two men were holding the rope.

pardes.body: Verses 2 to 11 are one man at night; verses 12 to 21 are the sea at the exodus. The join is {{12.0}}, a plain future verb, I will call to mind. Read the two halves as one argument and the logic is this: the speaker has asked whether God has changed, and instead of an answer he sets a piece of the past in front of himself and looks at it until the question loses its force. Notice what the second half does not do. It never mentions the speaker's distress, never says he slept, never claims the questions were wrong. The last verse ends on Moses and Aaron and simply stops.

Verse 11 is the crux and it is genuinely disputed. {{11.1}} is read by some as a noun from the root for sickness, giving this is my sickness, and by others as a form of the verb for entreating, giving this is my plea. {{11.3}} is equally open: the same consonants give either the plural construct of year, hence the years of the right hand, or an infinitive of the verb to change, hence the changing of the right hand. Translations pick one silently; the Hebrew does not. A second ambiguity sits in {{2.7}}, whose form can be read as a past tense, He gave ear, or as an infinitive continuing the cry. The storm of verses 18 to 20 shares vocabulary and images with the theophany in Habakkuk chapter 3, closely enough that the two texts are usually discussed together.

One reading takes the psalm as a description of how prayer actually works when nothing is going well. The four cohortatives are the mechanism: the first two, in verses 4 and 7, are memory turned on the self and they make things worse; the second two, in verses 12 and 13, are memory turned on an event outside the self and they hold. On this reading the cure is not new information but a change of object. A second reading works on the last two verses. {{20.5}} says the footprints were not known and {{21.3}} says it happened by the hand of Moses and Aaron, so the sentence that denies any visible trace is immediately followed by the two visible men who led the march. Where a path leaves no mark, the people who walked at the front are the only evidence there was one.

In kabbalistic vocabulary the right hand is the side of chesed, expansive kindness, and the left is the side of judgment and restraint. Verse 11 as usually vocalized asks about the years of the right hand, which makes the whole complaint a complaint about kindness that has stopped flowing, and verse 9 has already named chesed explicitly. The second half then answers in the register of concealment rather than of supply: the way exists, it runs through the sea, and it leaves no footprints. Water in this reading is the covering itself, and the split at the exodus is the one moment when the covering opened and the road underneath became briefly visible to everyone standing on the shore.
